questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: For a cell, the graph of the potential difference V across its terminals (y-axis) against the current I drawn from it (x-axis) is a straight line that cuts the V-axis at 2.0 V and the I-axis at 4.0 A. The internal resistance of the cell is:

solution.concept: Terminal voltage V = ε − Ir: a straight line with intercept ε on the V-axis and slope −r
solution.explanation: At I = 0 the terminal voltage equals the emf, so ε = 2.0 V. The line reaches V = 0 when the terminals are short-circuited, at I = ε/r = 4.0 A. The internal resistance is the magnitude of the slope.
steps: V = ε − Ir → V-intercept = ε = 2.0 V
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 Ω inverts the ratio (I-intercept/V-intercept). 8.0 Ω multiplies the two intercepts. 4.0 Ω reads the current intercept as if it were the resistance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 2 Ω resistor and a 3 Ω resistor are connected in series across an ideal 10 V battery. The heat produced in the 3 Ω resistor in one minute is:

solution.concept: Joule heating H = I²Rt, with the series current fixed by the total resistance
solution.explanation: The same current flows through both resistors: I = 10/(2 + 3) = 2 A. The heat produced in the 3 Ω resistor in 60 s is I²Rt.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1200 J is the heat produced in both resistors together. 480 J is the heat in the 2 Ω resistor. 2000 J puts the full 10 V across the 3 Ω resistor.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy, power; combination of resistors - series and parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform wire AB, 100 cm long and of resistance 10 Ω, is connected in series with a 5 Ω resistor across an ideal 6 V battery. The potential difference between two points of the wire that are 30 cm apart is:

solution.concept: Ohm's law; a uniform wire has the same resistance per unit length everywhere
solution.explanation: The current is fixed by the total resistance of the circuit. A 30 cm length of the uniform wire has 30% of its resistance, and the potential difference across it is the current times that resistance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.8 V ignores the 5 Ω resistor and puts all 6 V across the wire. 4.0 V is the potential difference across the whole wire. 2.0 V is the potential difference across the 5 Ω resistor.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Four wires meet at a junction in a circuit carrying steady currents. Currents of 4 A and 3 A flow into the junction through two of the wires, and a current of 2 A flows out of it through the third wire. The current in the fourth wire is:

options.text: 9 A, flowing out of the junction
5 A, flowing out of the junction

solution.concept: Kirchhoff's junction rule: total current in = total current out
solution.explanation: With steady currents no charge piles up at the junction, so the currents flowing in must equal the currents flowing out.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 A adds every current regardless of direction. 1 A subtracts the two incoming currents. 5 A into the junction has the right size but would make the incoming total 12 A against 2 A out.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules
solution.final_answer: Option D: 5 A, flowing out of the junction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Wheatstone bridge, resistors P and Q are in series in one branch and R and S in series in the other; both branches are connected across a cell, and a galvanometer joins the P–Q junction to the R–S junction. The bridge is balanced (P/Q = R/S). Which one of the following changes, made on its own, will make the galvanometer show a deflection?

options.text: Replacing the cell by one of twice the emf
Replacing the galvanometer by one of higher resistance

solution.concept: Balance condition of the Wheatstone bridge: P/Q = R/S
solution.explanation: The balance condition involves only the ratios of the four resistances; it contains neither the emf of the cell nor the resistance of the galvanometer. Doubling P and S makes the left ratio 2P/Q and the right ratio R/(2S), so P/Q is now four times R/S and the bridge is unbalanced.
steps: Double P and S: 2P/Q ≠ R/2S → deflection
Double P and Q: 2P/2Q = P/Q → still balanced
solution.why_others_wrong: The cell's emf and the galvanometer's resistance do not appear in the balance condition, so changing them keeps the null. Doubling P and Q leaves the ratio P/Q unchanged.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge
solution.final_answer: Option C: Doubling both P and S

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The SI unit of resistivity, Ω m, expressed in terms of the SI base units (kg, m, s, A), is:

solution.concept: ρ = RA/l, and 1 Ω = 1 V/A
solution.explanation: 1 V = 1 J/C = kg m² s⁻² /(A s) = kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹, so 1 Ω = 1 V/A = kg m² s⁻³ A⁻². Multiplying by a metre gives the unit of resistivity.
steps: 1 Ω m = kg m³ s⁻³ A⁻²
solution.why_others_wrong: kg m² s⁻³ A⁻² is the ohm itself (resistance, not resistivity). kg m s⁻³ A⁻² divides the ohm by a metre instead of multiplying. kg⁻¹ m⁻³ s³ A² is the unit of conductivity, the reciprocal of resistivity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law (resistivity)
solution.final_answer: Option D: kg m³ s⁻³ A⁻²

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The resistance of a metal wire is 5.0 Ω at 50 °C and 6.0 Ω at 100 °C. Assuming that its resistance varies linearly with temperature, its resistance at 0 °C and its temperature coefficient of resistance referred to 0 °C are, respectively:

solution.concept: R_T = R₀(1 + αT): a straight line whose slope is αR₀
solution.explanation: The resistance rises by 1.0 Ω for 50 °C, i.e. 0.02 Ω per °C. Extrapolating back 50 °C from 5.0 Ω gives R₀. Since the slope equals αR₀, α (referred to 0 °C) is the slope divided by R₀.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.0 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹ divides the slope by the resistance at 50 °C, and 3.3 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹ by the resistance at 100 °C, instead of by R₀. 4.2 Ω and 3.7 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹ wrongly take the resistance as proportional to the absolute temperature.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', temperature dependence of resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Three 6 Ω resistors are connected in series between points A and B, in the order A–P (first resistor), P–Q (second resistor) and Q–B (third resistor). A wire of negligible resistance then joins A to Q, and another wire of negligible resistance joins P to B. The equivalent resistance between A and B is:

solution.concept: Points joined by a wire of negligible resistance are at the same potential and can be merged
solution.explanation: Because of the wires, A and Q are one node and P and B are another. Then the first resistor (A–P) runs from node A to node B, the second (P–Q) from node B to node A and the third (Q–B) from node A to node B: all three resistors are connected between A and B, i.e. in parallel.
steps: Each 6 Ω resistor is connected between A and B
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 Ω ignores the two wires. 6 Ω keeps only one resistor between A and B. Zero assumes A and B are shorted, but A and B are still joined only through resistors.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A battery of emf 12 V delivers the greatest possible power to an external resistor when the resistance of that resistor is 3 Ω. The internal resistance of the battery and the greatest power it can deliver to an external resistor are, respectively:

solution.concept: Maximum power transfer: the power in the external resistor is greatest when R = r, and then equals ε²/4r
solution.explanation: P = ε²R/(R + r)² is greatest when R = r, so r = 3 Ω. The current is then ε/2r = 2 A and the power in the external resistor is I²R.
steps: Maximum when R = r → r = 3 Ω
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 W is the total power generated by the battery (εI), half of which is lost in the internal resistance. 48 W is ε²/r, the power that would be generated on short circuit. 1.5 Ω and 24 W wrongly take r as half of R.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wire of metal A (resistivity 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m) is joined end to end with a wire of alloy B (resistivity 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m) of the same cross-sectional area, and a steady current flows through the two wires in series. The ratio of the magnitude of the electric field inside wire B to that inside wire A is:

solution.concept: Microscopic form of Ohm's law: E = ρj
solution.explanation: The current and the cross-sectional area are the same for both wires, so the current density j is the same. The electric field needed to drive that current density is proportional to the resistivity.
steps: j = I/A, same in both wires
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 assumes that the same current means the same field. 0.02 inverts the ratio. 7.1 takes a square root that has no place in E = ρj.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law (j = σE)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The coil of an electric heater is cut to half its length, and the remaining half is connected across the same mains supply. Neglecting any change of resistance with temperature, the heater now draws twice the power.
Reason (R): The power drawn by a resistor across a fixed potential difference is V²/R, and halving the length of a uniform coil halves its resistance.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Power P = V²/R at a fixed potential difference; R ∝ length
solution.explanation: Half the length of the same wire has half the resistance. With the same mains voltage, P = V²/R doubles. R states exactly these two facts, so it explains A.
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and together they give the doubling, so R is the correct explanation of A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy, power
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Kirchhoff's junction rule holds for steady currents because no charge accumulates at a junction.
Statement II: Kirchhoff's loop rule can be applied only to closed loops that contain at least one cell.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Basis of Kirchhoff's rules
solution.explanation: The junction rule expresses conservation of charge: in the steady state charge does not pile up at a junction, so the current in equals the current out (Statement I true). The loop rule says the algebraic sum of the changes in potential round any closed loop is zero, because the electrostatic potential is single-valued; it applies to every closed loop, whether or not the loop contains a cell (Statement II false).
steps: Junction rule: charge conservation, no accumulation → I true
Loop rule: valid for any closed loop → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: A loop made only of resistors also obeys the loop rule (the sum of the IR terms is zero), so Statement II is false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A uniform metal wire is connected across a fixed potential difference, and its temperature stays the same. Each change in List-I is made to the original wire (or the wire is replaced by another wire of the same material). Match each change with its effect on the current in List-II.

List-I:
A. The length is doubled, the cross-sectional area being unchanged
B. The diameter is doubled, the length being unchanged
C. Both the length and the diameter are doubled
D. The wire is stretched uniformly to twice its length (its volume being unchanged)

List-II:
I. Becomes half
II. Becomes four times
III. Becomes twice
IV. Becomes one-fourth

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: R = ρl/A with ρ fixed; I = V/R at a fixed potential difference
solution.explanation: The current is inversely proportional to R, i.e. proportional to A/l. Doubling the diameter makes the area four times. Stretching to twice the length at constant volume halves the area, so R becomes four times.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-I, B-III, ... treats the area as proportional to the diameter instead of its square. A-III, B-II, ... makes the current proportional to the length. A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III interchanges the last two cases.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law (resistivity)
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A 3 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor are connected in parallel, and this combination is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor across an ideal 12 V battery. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The equivalent resistance of the circuit is 4 Ω.
(b) The current in the 3 Ω resistor is 1 A.
(c) The potential difference across the 2 Ω resistor is 6 V.
(d) The power dissipated in the 6 Ω resistor is 6 W.
(e) The power supplied by the battery is 24 W.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Series–parallel reduction, current division and power
solution.explanation: 3 Ω ∥ 6 Ω = 2 Ω, so the total is 4 Ω (a true) and the battery current is 3 A. The 2 Ω resistor takes 6 V (c true), leaving 6 V across the parallel pair: 2 A in the 3 Ω resistor (b false) and 1 A in the 6 Ω resistor, which dissipates 6²/6 = 6 W (d true). The battery supplies 12 × 3 = 36 W (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (b) or (e) include a false statement; (c) and (d) only leaves out the true statement (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A rheostat of total resistance 100 Ω is used as a potential divider: its two ends are connected across an ideal 10 V battery and its sliding contact is set exactly at the middle of its length. A load resistor R_L is connected between the sliding contact and the negative end of the rheostat (i.e. across the lower half). The potential difference across R_L is found to be 4.0 V. The value of R_L is:

solution.concept: Loaded potential divider: the load is in parallel with the lower part of the divider
solution.explanation: The lower 50 Ω of the rheostat in parallel with R_L forms R_p, which is in series with the upper 50 Ω. The 10 V divides in the ratio R_p : 50, and R_p must take 4.0 V.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33.3 Ω is the parallel combination R_p, not the load itself. 200 Ω divides the voltage in proportion to the whole 100 Ω rheostat, forgetting that the upper half is in series. 20 Ω comes from inverting the parallel-combination formula wrongly.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A copper wire 0.90 m long consists of two parts of equal length: the first 0.45 m has a cross-sectional area of 1.0 mm² and the remaining 0.45 m an area of 2.0 mm². It carries a steady current of 3.2 A. Taking the number density of free electrons in copper as 8.0 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the time taken by an electron to drift from one end of the wire to the other is:

solution.concept: Drift speed v_d = I/(neA); the same current flows through both parts
solution.explanation: The drift speed is larger in the thinner part. The total drift time is the sum of the times spent in the two parts, each found from its own drift speed.
steps: Thick part: v₂ = 1.25 × 10⁻⁴ m/s → t₂ = 3600 s
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 h uses the drift speed of the thinner part for the whole wire, and 2.0 h that of the thicker part. 1.33 h divides the length by the average of the two drift speeds, which is not the correct average for equal distances.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Four points A, B, C and D are each joined to every other point by a separate resistor (six resistors in all, insulated where they cross). The resistors joining A–B, A–C, A–D, B–C and B–D are each 2 Ω, and the resistor joining C–D is 1 Ω. The equivalent resistance between A and B is:

solution.concept: Symmetry: points at the same potential carry no current between them
solution.explanation: With a potential difference between A and B, C and D are placed identically (each joined to A and to B by 2 Ω), so they are at the same potential and the C–D resistor carries no current, whatever its value. The network is then the direct 2 Ω resistor in parallel with two 4 Ω paths (A–C–B and A–D–B).
steps: V_C = V_D → no current in C–D
Paths: 2 Ω, 4 Ω, 4 Ω in parallel
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 Ω keeps only the direct A–B resistor. 4/3 Ω leaves out one of the two 4 Ω paths. 2/3 Ω treats each two-resistor path as a single 2 Ω resistor.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: When a cell is being charged by a current of 2.0 A, the potential difference across its terminals is 1.6 V. When the same cell is discharging and supplies a current of 2.0 A to an external circuit, the potential difference across its terminals is 1.2 V. The emf and internal resistance of the cell are, respectively:

solution.concept: Terminal voltage: V = ε + Ir while charging, V = ε − Ir while discharging
solution.explanation: While charging, the current is driven into the positive terminal against the emf, so the terminal voltage exceeds ε by Ir. While discharging it falls short of ε by Ir. Adding and subtracting the two equations gives ε and r.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.4 V and 0.2 Ω divides the difference of the two voltages by 2.0 A instead of by 4.0 A. 1.6 V and 1.2 V take one of the terminal voltages as the emf.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a single series circuit of a cell and several resistors, the current is largest in the resistor nearest the positive terminal of the cell and becomes smaller in each later resistor, because charge is used up as it flows.
Reason (R): In a series circuit carrying a steady current, the current is the same at every cross-section, because charge is conserved and does not accumulate anywhere in the circuit.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Steady current and conservation of charge
solution.explanation: Charge is not consumed in a resistor; it is energy that is converted into heat. In the steady state no charge accumulates anywhere, so the same current flows through every element of a series circuit (A false, R true).
steps: Charge is conserved; energy, not charge, is used up in resistors
Same current in all series elements
solution.why_others_wrong: A is the common misconception that current is 'used up'. R is the correct statement, so the options that call A true are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electric current; Kirchhoff's rules
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A cell X (emf 6 V, internal resistance 1 Ω) and a cell Y (emf 4 V, internal resistance 1 Ω) are connected in parallel, positive terminal to positive terminal and negative terminal to negative terminal. Nothing else is connected to them. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) A current of 1 A flows round the loop formed by the two cells.
(b) The potential difference between the common positive and common negative terminals is 5 V.
(c) The current flows out of the positive terminal of Y.
(d) Heat is produced in the two cells at a total rate of 2 W.
(e) Cell X converts chemical energy into electrical energy at the rate of 4 W.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Loop rule for two opposing emfs; charging of the weaker cell
solution.explanation: Round the loop the emfs oppose each other: I = (6 − 4)/(1 + 1) = 1 A (a true). The common terminal voltage is 6 − 1 × 1 = 5 V = 4 + 1 × 1 (b true). Since 5 V exceeds Y's emf, the current is driven into Y's positive terminal and Y is being charged (c false). Heat in the internal resistances is 1² × 1 + 1² × 1 = 2 W (d true). X converts chemical energy at ε_X I = 6 W, of which 4 W is stored in Y and 2 W is heat (e false).
steps: Current enters Y at + → Y charged
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (c) or (e) include a false statement; (a) and (b) only leaves out the true statement (d).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance; Kirchhoff's rules

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: The magnetic field at a distance d from a long straight wire carrying a steady current I is B. If the current is doubled, the magnetic field at a distance 3d from the wire is:

solution.concept: Field of a long straight wire: B = µ₀I/(2πr), i.e. B ∝ I/r
solution.explanation: The field is directly proportional to the current and inversely proportional to the distance from the wire.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6B multiplies by the distance ratio instead of dividing. 2B/9 treats the field as falling off as 1/r². 3B/2 inverts the result.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field due to a long straight current-carrying wire

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A shunt of 2 Ω is connected across a galvanometer, and it is found that only 10% of the main current now passes through the galvanometer. The resistance of the galvanometer is:

solution.concept: Galvanometer and shunt are in parallel: the currents divide inversely as the resistances
solution.explanation: The potential difference across the galvanometer equals that across the shunt. 10% of the current flows through G and 90% through S.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.22 Ω inverts the current ratio (it would make the galvanometer carry 90%). 20 Ω divides S by 0.1 without using the 90% through the shunt. 1.8 Ω multiplies S by 0.9 instead of by 9.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', moving coil galvanometer

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A plane circular loop of area 0.02 m² carries a steady current of 5 A. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.3 T with its plane perpendicular to the field. The magnitude of the torque on the loop is:

solution.concept: Torque on a current loop: τ = m × B, of magnitude mB sin θ (θ = angle between m and B)
solution.explanation: The magnetic moment of a plane loop is perpendicular to its plane. With the plane perpendicular to B, the moment is parallel (or antiparallel) to B, so θ = 0 (or 180°) and the torque is zero.
steps: m = IA = 5 × 0.02 = 0.1 A m², along the normal to the loop
Plane ⊥ B → m ∥ B → sin θ = 0
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.03 N m is the maximum torque mB, which acts when the plane of the loop is parallel to the field. 0.015 N m and 0.026 N m correspond to angles of 30° and 60° between m and B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', torque on current loop, magnetic dipole

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Ampere's circuital law, ∮B·dl = µ₀I, holds for any closed path in a region of steady currents. It is, however, practically useful for calculating the magnetic field only when:

options.text: the closed path chosen is a circle
the closed path chosen encloses no current
the current distribution is symmetric enough that a closed path can be chosen along which the field is tangential and of constant magnitude (or zero)

solution.concept: Ampere's circuital law and its use for symmetric current distributions
solution.explanation: The law always relates the line integral of B round a closed path to the current enclosed. To get B itself out of the integral, the path must be one on which B is tangential with a constant magnitude (as for a long straight wire, a solenoid or a toroid), so that ∮B·dl reduces to B × (length of the path).
steps: B can be taken out of the integral only on a symmetric path
So the law is useful when there is high symmetry
solution.why_others_wrong: The law in this form is for steady currents, not time-varying ones. The path need not be a circle (a rectangle is used for the solenoid). A path enclosing no current gives ∮B·dl = 0, which by itself does not give B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law
solution.final_answer: Option D: the current distribution is symmetric enough that a closed path can be chosen along which the field is tangential and of constant magnitude (or zero)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A current-carrying solenoid behaves like a bar magnet; the end at which the current is seen to flow anticlockwise, when viewed from outside facing that end, acts as its north pole.
Statement II: The magnetic field lines of a bar magnet and those of a current-carrying solenoid form continuous closed loops.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid
solution.explanation: By the right-hand rule, an anticlockwise current seen from one end produces a field pointing out of that end, towards the viewer, so field lines emerge there: it is a north pole (Statement I true). Magnetic field lines never begin or end; for both the bar magnet and the solenoid they run outside from N to S and inside from S to N, forming closed loops (Statement II true).
steps: Anticlockwise current facing the viewer → field towards the viewer → N pole
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are correct, so options calling either of them false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet; bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
A positively charged particle moves through a uniform magnetic field. Its velocity and the field are along the directions given in List-I. Match each case with the direction of the magnetic force on the particle in List-II.

List-I:
A. Velocity along +x, field along +y
B. Velocity along +y, field along +z
C. Velocity along +z, field along +x
D. Velocity along +x, field along +z

List-II:
I. Along +x
II. Along +y
III. Along +z
IV. Along −y

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Magnetic force F = q(v × B)
solution.explanation: For a positive charge the force is along v × B. Using x̂ × ŷ = ẑ, ŷ × ẑ = x̂, ẑ × x̂ = ŷ and x̂ × ẑ = −ŷ gives the four directions.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes take B × v instead of v × B for some cases, which reverses the force, or interchange the results of two cases.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two long straight parallel wires P and Q, 20 cm apart, carry steady currents of 2 A and 6 A respectively, in opposite directions. In the plane containing the two wires, the resultant magnetic field due to them is zero at a line that is:

options.text: 5 cm from P, between the wires
10 cm from P, on the side of P away from Q
10 cm from Q, on the side of Q away from P
nowhere; no such line exists in that plane

solution.concept: Superposition of the fields of two long straight wires (B = µ₀I/2πr)
solution.explanation: For opposite currents, the two fields point the same way at every point between the wires, so they can cancel only outside. The point must be nearer the smaller current so that its field can match the larger current's field from farther away.
steps: Outside, beyond P, distance x from P: 2/x = 6/(x + 20)
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 cm from P between the wires is the answer for currents in the same direction. A point beyond Q is nearer the larger current, so the fields cannot cancel there. A null line does exist, outside the wires on P's side.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field due to a long straight current-carrying wire
solution.final_answer: Option B: 10 cm from P, on the side of P away from Q

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A single circular loop of wire of radius 10 cm carries a steady current, and the magnetic field at its centre is 2π × 10⁻⁵ T. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnetic dipole moment of the loop is about:

solution.concept: B at the centre = µ₀I/2R; magnetic moment m = IA
solution.explanation: First find the current from the field at the centre, then multiply it by the area of the loop.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.63 A m² uses µ₀I/4R (the field of a semicircle), which doubles the current. 0.16 A m² uses µ₀I/R, which halves it. 0.10 A m² leaves out π from the area.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop; the magnetic dipole moment

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two long straight parallel wires, 10 cm apart, each carry a steady current of 10 A in the same direction. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at a point that is 10 cm from each wire (so that the point and the two wires form an equilateral triangle in a plane perpendicular to the wires) is about:

solution.concept: Vector superposition of the fields of two long straight wires
solution.explanation: Each wire produces 2 × 10⁻⁵ T at the point, perpendicular to the line joining that wire to the point. The two lines are at 60° to each other, and for currents in the same direction the two field vectors are also at 60°, giving a resultant of 2B cos 30° = √3 B.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T adds the magnitudes as if the fields were parallel. 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ T is the result for currents in opposite directions (fields at 120°). The fields do not cancel at this point.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field due to a long straight current-carrying wire

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Three long straight parallel wires lie in one plane, equally spaced 10 cm apart, and each carries a steady current of 10 A in the same direction. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitude of the net magnetic force per unit length on one of the outer wires is:

solution.concept: Force per unit length between parallel currents: f = µ₀I₁I₂/(2πd), attractive for currents in the same direction
solution.explanation: An outer wire is attracted by the middle wire (10 cm away) and by the other outer wire (20 cm away). Both forces point towards the other wires, so they add.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 × 10⁻⁴ N/m places the far wire at 10 cm. 2 × 10⁻⁴ N/m leaves out the far wire. Zero is the net force on the middle wire, not on an outer one.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force between two parallel currents, the ampere

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A charged particle moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. If its kinetic energy is doubled, the field being unchanged, then:

options.text: the radius doubles and the time period of revolution is unchanged
the radius becomes √2 times and the time period of revolution is unchanged
the radius becomes √2 times and the time period becomes 1/√2 times
the radius is unchanged and the time period is halved

solution.concept: r = mv/(qB) = √(2mK)/(qB); T = 2πm/(qB)
solution.explanation: Doubling the kinetic energy makes the speed √2 times. The radius is proportional to the speed, so it becomes √2 times. The period does not depend on the speed at all.
solution.why_others_wrong: The radius is proportional to the speed (√K), not to K. The period depends only on m, q and B, so it does not change.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field
solution.final_answer: Option B: the radius becomes √2 times and the time period of revolution is unchanged

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a steady current is passed through a loosely wound, flexible long solenoid, the solenoid tends to contract along its length.
Reason (R): Adjacent turns of the solenoid carry currents in the same direction, and parallel currents in the same direction attract each other.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Force between parallel currents
solution.explanation: Neighbouring turns of a solenoid are side by side and their currents flow the same way round. Parallel currents in the same direction attract, so the turns pull towards one another and the solenoid shortens. R explains A.
steps: Adjacent turns: currents in the same direction
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the attraction between neighbouring turns is the cause of the contraction, so R is the correct explanation of A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force between two parallel currents, the ampere
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
A long, straight, thin-walled hollow metal tube of radius R carries a steady current I along its length, the current being spread uniformly round its circumference. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The magnetic field is zero at every point in the hollow space inside the tube.
(b) At a distance r (r > R) from the axis, the magnitude of the field is µ₀I/(2πr).
(c) If the current in the tube is doubled, the field inside the hollow space becomes non-zero.
(d) Outside the tube, the magnetic field lines are circles centred on the axis of the tube.
(e) At a fixed distance r (r > R) from the axis, the field depends on the radius R of the tube.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Ampere's circuital law with a circular Amperian loop coaxial with the tube
solution.explanation: A circular loop of radius r < R inside the hollow space encloses no current, so B × 2πr = 0 and B = 0 for any current (a true, c false). A loop of radius r > R encloses the whole current I, so B = µ₀I/(2πr), the same as for a thin wire on the axis and independent of R (b true, e false). By symmetry the field lines outside are circles centred on the axis (d true).
steps: r > R: B × 2πr = µ₀I → B = µ₀I/2πr
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (c) or (e) include a false statement; (a) and (b) only leaves out the true statement (d).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: At large distances, the magnetic field lines of a bar magnet have the same pattern as the electric field lines of an electric dipole.
Statement II: Like the electric field lines of an electric dipole, the magnetic field lines of a bar magnet begin on its north pole and end on its south pole.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Bar magnet as a magnetic dipole; magnetic field lines form closed loops
solution.explanation: Far from a bar magnet, its field has the same form as the field of an electric dipole, with m in place of p and µ₀/4π in place of 1/4πε₀ (Statement I true). But magnetic field lines do not begin or end anywhere: they pass through the magnet from S to N and form continuous closed loops, unlike electric field lines, which begin on positive charges and end on negative charges (Statement II false).
steps: Far field of a bar magnet ≅ dipole field → I true
Magnetic field lines are closed loops → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II describes electric field lines; magnetic field lines continue inside the magnet, so it is false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet (the electrostatic analog; magnetic field lines)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long straight hollow cylindrical conductor has an inner radius of 2.0 cm and an outer radius of 4.0 cm. It carries a steady current of 6.0 A along its length, spread uniformly over the cross-section of its wall. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitude of the magnetic field at a distance of 3.0 cm from its axis is about:

solution.concept: Ampere's circuital law: B × 2πr = µ₀ × (current enclosed by the circle of radius r)
solution.explanation: The current density is uniform over the annular cross-section, so the current enclosed by a circle of radius r is in proportion to the area of the wall inside that circle: (r² − a²)/(b² − a²) of the total.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T uses the whole 6.0 A. 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ T takes the enclosed current in proportion to (r − a)/(b − a) instead of the areas. Zero would be correct only in the hollow region (r < 2.0 cm).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two parallel conducting rails, 0.50 m apart, lie on a smooth plane inclined at 45° to the horizontal, running straight down the slope. A metal rod of mass 0.10 kg rests across the rails, horizontal and perpendicular to them. A uniform vertical magnetic field of 0.50 T acts in the region. Taking g = 10 m/s², the current that must be passed through the rod, in the proper direction, to keep it at rest is:

options.text: zero, because a vertical field cannot push the rod along the slope

solution.concept: Force on a current-carrying rod F = BIL; equilibrium on a smooth incline
solution.explanation: The rod is horizontal and the field vertical, so the magnetic force BIL is horizontal and perpendicular to the rod. Its component up the slope is BIL cos 45°, which must balance the component of the weight down the slope, mg sin 45°.
steps: BIL cos θ = mg sin θ
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.8 A balances mg sin θ with the whole of BIL, as if the magnetic force acted along the slope. 5.7 A balances BIL cos θ against the whole weight. A horizontal force does have a component along the slope, so zero is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A galvanometer in series with a 100 Ω resistor gives full-scale deflection when a potential difference of 1.0 V is applied across the combination. With a 400 Ω resistor in place of the 100 Ω resistor, full-scale deflection needs 2.5 V. The resistance of the galvanometer and its full-scale current are, respectively:

solution.concept: Galvanometer as a voltmeter: V = I_g(G + R)
solution.explanation: The same full-scale current I_g flows in both cases. Subtracting the two equations eliminates G.
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 Ω is G + 100, the total resistance in the first case. 10 mA divides 1.0 V by the 100 Ω resistor alone. 60 Ω and 6.25 mA take I_g as 2.5 V/400 Ω, ignoring the galvanometer's own resistance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', moving coil galvanometer

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A proton (mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moving with a speed of 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s enters a region of uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T, its velocity being perpendicular to the field. The time it takes for its direction of motion to turn through 90°, and the magnitude of its displacement during this time, are:

solution.concept: Circular motion in a magnetic field: r = mv/(qB), angular speed ω = qB/m
solution.explanation: The velocity turns at the constant rate ω = qB/m, so turning through π/2 takes a quarter of the period. In that time the proton moves along a quarter circle, and its displacement is the chord joining the ends of the quarter circle, √2 r.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.3 cm is the length of the quarter-circle arc (distance travelled), not the displacement. 2π × 10⁻⁸ s is half a period. 4π × 10⁻⁸ s and 8.0 cm are the full period and the diameter.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field
solution.final_answer: Option A: π × 10⁻⁸ s and 5.7 cm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Using a spring of smaller torsional constant k in a moving-coil galvanometer increases its current sensitivity but decreases its voltage sensitivity.
Reason (R): Both the current sensitivity (NAB/k) and the voltage sensitivity (NAB/kR) of a moving-coil galvanometer are inversely proportional to k.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Current sensitivity φ/I = NAB/k; voltage sensitivity φ/V = NAB/(kR)
solution.explanation: Making k smaller increases both sensitivities, because both contain k in the denominator and the coil's resistance R is not changed by changing the spring. A is therefore false, while R is a correct statement.
solution.why_others_wrong: A confuses the spring with the number of turns: increasing N raises R as well, which is why it does not raise the voltage sensitivity. Changing k leaves R unchanged, so both sensitivities rise.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', moving coil galvanometer
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
A short bar magnet of magnetic moment m is placed with its centre at the origin. Writing k = µ₀/4π and ignoring all other magnetic fields, match each point in List-I with the magnitude of the field there in List-II.

List-I:
A. On the axis of the magnet, at a distance r from its centre
B. On the equatorial line (perpendicular bisector of the axis), at a distance r from the centre
C. On the axis of the magnet, at a distance 2r from its centre
D. On the equatorial line, at a distance 2r from the centre

List-II:
I. km/r³
II. 2km/r³
III. km/(8r³)
IV. km/(4r³)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Field of a short magnet: axial 2km/r³, equatorial km/r³ (both ∝ 1/r³)
solution.explanation: At equal distances the axial field is twice the equatorial field. Doubling the distance divides each by 2³ = 8.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV interchanges the axial and equatorial fields. A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV forgets the factor 2 of the axial field at 2r and so interchanges the two values at 2r. A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III mixes up the fields at r and at 2r on the equatorial line.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet (field of a magnetic dipole)
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The magnetic flux linked with a single-turn closed loop varies with time as Φ = (3t² − 4t) mWb, where t is in seconds. The magnitude of the emf induced in the loop at t = 2 s is:

solution.concept: Faraday's law: ε = −dΦ/dt
solution.explanation: The induced emf depends on the rate of change of the flux at that instant, not on the flux itself.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 mV is the value of the flux at t = 2 s, not its rate of change. 12 mV differentiates only the 3t² term. 2 mV divides the flux by the time.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A flexible circular conducting loop lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T. Its radius is increasing at a steady rate of 2.0 mm/s. The magnitude of the emf induced in the loop at the instant when its radius is 10 cm is about:

solution.concept: Faraday's law with a changing area: ε = B dA/dt
solution.explanation: The field is constant, so the flux changes only because the area πr² changes. dA/dt = 2πr (dr/dt).
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.31 mV takes dA/dt as πr dr/dt (dropping the factor 2 of the derivative of r²). 0.10 mV leaves out 2π. 1.3 mV doubles the correct value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a given rate of change of magnetic flux through a closed coil, the induced emf does not depend on the resistance of the coil, but the induced current does.
Statement II: An emf is induced by a changing magnetic flux only if the loop through which the flux changes is made of a conducting material.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Faraday's law gives the emf; the current follows from Ohm's law
solution.explanation: The induced emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage, whatever the coil is made of; the current is this emf divided by the resistance (Statement I true). The emf is induced round any closed path through which the flux changes; a conducting loop is needed only for a current to flow (Statement II false).
steps: Emf exists even without a conductor
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II confuses the emf with the current: a non-conducting ring has the same emf but no current.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The magnetic flux through a closed coil of fixed resistance increases steadily (linearly) with time from zero. While the flux is increasing, the current induced in the coil:

options.text: is zero, because the flux starts from zero

solution.concept: Faraday's law: the emf depends on the rate of change of flux
solution.explanation: A flux that rises linearly has a constant rate of change, so the induced emf is constant, and with a fixed resistance so is the current.
solution.why_others_wrong: The current follows the rate of change of the flux, not the flux itself, so it neither grows with the flux nor is zero when the flux starts from zero. A constant rate gives no decrease.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction
solution.final_answer: Option D: is constant and non-zero

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A metal rod 0.4 m long rotates with an angular speed of 20 rad/s about an axis passing through its midpoint and perpendicular to the rod. A uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T acts parallel to the axis of rotation. The potential difference between the two ends of the rod is:

solution.concept: Motional emf of a rotating rod: ε = ½Bωl² between the axis and the end of a length l
solution.explanation: Each half of the rod (length 0.2 m) has an emf ½Bω(0.2)² = 0.2 V between the midpoint and its outer end. Both outer ends are at the same potential relative to the midpoint (both higher, or both lower), so the potential difference between the two ends is zero.
steps: Each half: ½ × 0.5 × 20 × 0.2² = 0.2 V, midpoint to end
Both ends are 0.2 V from the midpoint in the same sense
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.8 V is the emf for rotation about one end. 0.2 V is the potential difference between the midpoint and either end. 0.4 V adds the two halves as if they were in series.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', motional electromotive force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A resistor and an inductor are connected in series to an AC source. At a source frequency of 50 Hz the power factor of the circuit is 0.80. If the frequency is changed to 100 Hz, the components and the source voltage being unchanged, the power factor becomes about:

solution.concept: Power factor of an LR circuit: cos φ = R/√(R² + X_L²), with X_L = ωL ∝ f
solution.explanation: A power factor of 0.80 means R : X_L = 4 : 3 at 50 Hz. Doubling the frequency doubles X_L but leaves R unchanged.
steps: At 50 Hz: R = 4k, X_L = 3k (so that cos φ = 4/5)
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.40 halves the power factor, as if it were inversely proportional to the frequency. 0.94 halves X_L, as for a capacitor. 0.80 assumes the power factor does not depend on frequency.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', LCR series circuit (impedance, phase); power in AC circuit: the power factor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The mutual inductance of a pair of coils is 0.10 H. The current in the first coil varies as i₁ = 2.0 sin(100πt) A, with t in seconds. The peak value of the emf induced in the second coil is about:

solution.concept: Mutual induction: ε₂ = −M di₁/dt
solution.explanation: Differentiating i₁ = I₀ sin ωt gives I₀ω cos ωt, so the induced emf oscillates with peak value MI₀ω.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.20 V is MI₀, without the factor ω. 20 V uses ω = 100 instead of 100π rad/s. 44.4 V is the rms value of the emf, not its peak.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', inductance (mutual inductance)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When the load connected to the secondary of an ideal transformer draws a larger current, the current drawn by the primary from the supply also increases.
Reason (R): An ideal transformer is 100% efficient only when no load is connected to its secondary.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Ideal transformer: output power = input power, V_s I_s = V_p I_p
solution.explanation: For an ideal transformer the input power equals the output power at every load, and the voltages are fixed by the supply and the turns ratio. A larger secondary current therefore means a larger primary current, I_p = (V_s/V_p) I_s (A true). An ideal transformer has no losses at any load, so R is false.
steps: Ideal: 100% efficient at every load → R false
solution.why_others_wrong: R is false: 'ideal' means no losses whatever the load. So the options that call R true are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', transformers
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In an AC generator, the ends of the rotating coil are connected to the external circuit through slip rings and brushes.
Statement II: The frequency of the alternating emf produced by an AC generator does not depend on the number of turns in its coil.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: AC generator: ε = NBAω sin ωt
solution.explanation: The coil turns continuously, so its ends are connected to rotating slip rings on which fixed carbon brushes press, connecting the coil to the outside circuit (Statement I true). The emf varies as sin ωt, where ω is the angular speed of rotation; the number of turns N affects only the amplitude NBAω (Statement II true).
steps: Slip rings + brushes connect the rotating coil → I true
Frequency = ω/2π; N changes only the peak emf → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are correct, so options calling either of them false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', AC generator
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each physical quantity in List-I with an equivalent form of its SI unit in List-II.

List-I:
A. Inductance
B. Magnetic flux
C. Reactance
D. Capacitance

List-II:
I. V s
II. V s A⁻¹
III. A s V⁻¹
IV. V A⁻¹

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Units from defining relations: ε = −dΦ/dt, ε = −L dI/dt, X = V/I, C = Q/V
solution.explanation: From ε = −dΦ/dt, flux has the unit of emf × time, V s (the weber). From ε = −L dI/dt, inductance has the unit V s A⁻¹ (the henry). A reactance is a ratio of voltage to current, V A⁻¹ (ohm). Capacitance is charge per unit voltage, A s V⁻¹ (farad).
solution.why_others_wrong: A-I, B-II, ... interchanges the units of inductance and flux. A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV interchanges reactance and capacitance. A-IV, ... gives inductance the unit of resistance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', inductance; Faraday's law of induction
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A square conducting loop of side 10 cm and resistance 0.50 Ω lies in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T, which fills the region on one side of a straight boundary. Initially the loop is entirely inside the field with one side lying along the boundary. It is pulled out of the field, perpendicular to the boundary, at a constant speed of 2.0 m/s. The work that must be done to pull it completely out of the field is:

options.text: zero, because the speed is constant

solution.concept: Motional emf ε = BLv; opposing force BIL; work = force × distance (equal to the heat produced)
solution.explanation: While the loop is leaving, only the side still in the field cuts field lines, so ε = BLv. The induced current produces a force BIL opposing the motion, and an equal external force is needed to keep the speed constant over a distance equal to the side L.
solution.why_others_wrong: At constant speed the applied force balances the magnetic drag, it is not zero, so work is done (and appears as heat). 2.0 mJ takes the emf as 2BLv, as if two sides cut the field. 0.5 mJ uses half the force, as if the force grew from zero.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', motional electromotive force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A coil (having both resistance and inductance) is connected in series with a capacitor across an AC source of rms voltage 100 V, and the frequency is adjusted to resonance. An AC voltmeter connected across the capacitor then reads 240 V. The reading of the voltmeter when it is connected across the coil is:

solution.concept: Series resonance: V_L = V_C, and the source voltage appears across the resistance; phasor addition
solution.explanation: At resonance the inductive and capacitive voltages cancel, so the whole 100 V of the source is across the coil's resistance. The coil's inductive voltage equals the capacitor voltage, 240 V, and it is 90° ahead of the resistive voltage, so the two add as phasors.
steps: At resonance: V_R = V_source = 100 V, V_L = V_C = 240 V
solution.why_others_wrong: 240 V ignores the coil's resistance. 340 V adds the two voltages arithmetically, and 140 V subtracts them, ignoring the 90° phase difference.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit (resonance)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A long solenoid of radius 2.0 cm has 2000 turns per metre. A coil of 100 turns and radius 5.0 cm is placed around the middle of the solenoid, coaxial with it. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the mutual inductance of the solenoid and the coil is about:

options.text: zero, because the coil lies outside the solenoid, where the field is zero

solution.concept: Mutual inductance M = N₂Φ₂/I₁, with the flux of the long solenoid confined to its own cross-section
solution.explanation: A current I in the solenoid produces B = µ₀nI inside it and practically zero field outside. The flux through each turn of the larger coil is therefore B × (area of the solenoid), not B × (area of the coil). The coil surrounds the solenoid, so all of this flux links it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 mH uses the area of the coil, but there is no field between the solenoid and the coil. 0.10 mH leaves π out of the area. The coil does lie in the field-free region, but it encircles the solenoid's flux, so the flux linkage is not zero.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', inductance (mutual inductance)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A conducting rod slides with a constant velocity v along two parallel, frictionless conducting rails that are joined at one end through a resistor R. A uniform magnetic field B acts perpendicular to the plane of the rails. An external agent keeps the velocity constant; the rod and rails have negligible resistance. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The mechanical power supplied by the external agent equals the rate at which heat is produced in R.
(b) The magnetic force on the rod due to the induced current opposes its motion.
(c) If the resistor is removed so that the circuit is open, the emf between the ends of the rod becomes zero.
(d) Doubling the speed of the rod makes the rate of heating in R four times as large.
(e) Doubling the magnetic field doubles the external force needed to keep the speed constant.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Motional emf ε = Blv; energy conservation and Lenz's law
solution.explanation: The induced current I = Blv/R gives a force F = BIl = B²l²v/R opposing the motion (b true, Lenz's law), so the agent supplies power Fv = B²l²v²/R, equal to I²R (a true). The heating rate ∝ v² (d true) and the force ∝ B² (e false: it becomes four times). The emf Blv exists across the moving rod whether or not a current flows (c false).
steps: Open circuit: emf Blv, current zero
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (c) or (e) include a false statement; (a) and (b) only leaves out the true statement (d).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', motional electromotive force; Lenz's law and conservation of energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Visible sunlight absorbed by the Earth's surface is re-radiated, and part of this re-radiated energy is trapped by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, keeping the Earth warm (the greenhouse effect). The radiation re-emitted by the Earth's surface is mainly:

solution.concept: Infrared waves and the greenhouse effect
solution.explanation: The Earth's surface, being much cooler than the Sun, re-radiates the absorbed energy at longer wavelengths, in the infrared. Greenhouse gases absorb this infrared radiation and so keep the Earth warm.
steps: Re-emitted by the cooler surface: longer wavelengths → infrared
solution.why_others_wrong: Ultraviolet and X-rays have shorter wavelengths than visible light; a cool surface does not emit them. Microwaves are not the radiation by which the warm surface mainly re-radiates.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum (infrared waves)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: While a parallel-plate capacitor is being charged, the charge on its positive plate varies with time as q = (2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C s⁻²) t². The displacement current in the region between the plates at t = 3.0 s is:

options.text: zero, because no charge crosses the gap between the plates

solution.concept: Displacement current i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt, which equals the conduction current dq/dt in the leads
solution.explanation: Between the plates the electric flux is q/ε₀, so ε₀ dΦ_E/dt = dq/dt: the displacement current between the plates equals the rate at which charge is building up on the plates.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 µA is the numerical value of the charge (18 µC) at t = 3.0 s, not its rate of change. 6 µA is the average current q/t over the first 3 s. No charge crosses the gap, but the changing electric field gives a displacement current equal to the conduction current.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', displacement current

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a plane electromagnetic wave travelling through vacuum, the oscillating electric and magnetic fields at any point reach their maximum values at the same instant.
Reason (R): Electromagnetic waves are transverse: the electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the wave.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Plane EM wave: E_x = E₀ sin(kz − ωt), B_y = B₀ sin(kz − ωt)
solution.explanation: In a plane wave in vacuum, E and B vary with the same phase (kz − ωt), so they are in phase and have their maxima together, with E₀ = cB₀ (A true). The fields are also perpendicular to the direction of propagation (R true). But being transverse is a statement about directions; it does not say anything about the relative phase of E and B, so R does not explain A.
steps: Same phase (kz − ωt) for E and B → A true
E, B ⊥ direction of propagation → R true
Direction (R) ≠ phase (A) → R not the explanation
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, but the transverse nature of the wave concerns the directions of the fields, not the instants at which they peak, so R is not the explanation of A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves (nature of electromagnetic waves)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A plane electromagnetic wave of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz travels through a transparent, non-magnetic medium. The amplitudes of its electric and magnetic fields are 30 V/m and 1.5 × 10⁻⁷ T. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the refractive index of the medium and the wavelength of the wave in the medium are, respectively:

solution.concept: In a medium, E₀/B₀ = v (the wave speed in the medium); n = c/v; λ = v/f
solution.explanation: The ratio of the field amplitudes gives the speed of the wave in the medium. The refractive index is c/v, and the wavelength in the medium is v/f (the frequency is the same as in vacuum).
solution.why_others_wrong: 600 nm is the wavelength in vacuum (c/f). 0.67 is v/c, the reciprocal of the refractive index. 900 nm multiplies the vacuum wavelength by n instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ray of light in air falls at an angle of incidence of 60° on the plane surface of a transparent medium of refractive index √(3/2) (about 1.22). Part of the light is reflected and part is refracted. The angle between the reflected ray and the refracted ray is:

solution.concept: Law of reflection and Snell's law
solution.explanation: The reflected ray makes 60° with the normal on the air side. Snell's law gives the angle of refraction. The two rays lie on opposite sides of the surface, so the angle between them is 180° − (angle of reflection + angle of refraction).
solution.why_others_wrong: 105° adds the two angles made with the normal. 15° is the deviation of the refracted ray (i − r). 90° would be correct only at the polarising (Brewster) angle, which here is not 60°.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A plane wavefront of light travelling in air (speed 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s) meets the plane surface of a glass block. The incident wavefront makes an angle of 60° with the surface, and the refracted wavefront inside the glass makes an angle of 30° with the surface. The speed of light in the glass is about:

solution.concept: Refraction of a plane wave by Huygens' construction: sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂
solution.explanation: The angle between a wavefront and the surface equals the angle between the corresponding ray and the normal, so i = 60° and r = 30°. In the time the incident wavefront moves a distance v₁t in air, the secondary wavelet in glass grows to radius v₂t, which gives sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.2 × 10⁸ m/s inverts the ratio and exceeds the speed of light in vacuum. 1.5 × 10⁸ m/s uses the ratio of the angles (30°/60°) instead of their sines. 2.6 × 10⁸ m/s multiplies by cos 30° instead of using the sine ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', refraction and reflection of plane waves using Huygens principle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In Young's double-slit experiment the fringe width is 0.5 mm. If the separation between the slits is halved and the distance between the slits and the screen is doubled, the wavelength being unchanged, the new fringe width is:

solution.concept: Fringe width β = λD/d
solution.explanation: The fringe width is proportional to D and inversely proportional to d. Doubling D doubles β, and halving d doubles it again.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.5 mm assumes the two changes cancel. 1.0 mm applies only one of the two changes. 0.125 mm takes β as proportional to d and inversely proportional to D.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', interference of light waves and Young's experiment

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Light of wavelength 600 nm in vacuum passes normally through a glass plate 1.0 mm thick, of refractive index 1.5. The number of wavelengths of the light contained in the thickness of the plate is:

solution.concept: On entering a medium of refractive index n, the frequency is unchanged and the wavelength becomes λ₀/n
solution.explanation: Inside the glass the wavelength is 600/1.5 = 400 nm. The number of wavelengths in the plate is its thickness divided by this wavelength.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1667 uses the vacuum wavelength. 1111 multiplies the wavelength by n instead of dividing. 3750 multiplies the correct number by n once more.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A plane wavefront travelling along the principal axis falls on a concave mirror of small aperture. The reflected wavefront is:

options.text: spherical, converging to the focus of the mirror
plane, travelling back along the axis
spherical, diverging from a point behind the mirror
cylindrical, converging to a line through the pole

solution.concept: Wavefronts and rays: rays are normal to wavefronts
solution.explanation: A concave mirror reflects rays parallel to its axis so that they converge to its focus. The surfaces normal to these converging rays are spheres centred on the focus, shrinking as they approach it: a converging spherical wavefront.
steps: Wavefront ⊥ rays → spherical, centred on F, converging
solution.why_others_wrong: A plane mirror would return a plane wavefront. A diverging spherical wavefront from a point behind the mirror is produced by a convex mirror. A spherical mirror does not produce a cylindrical wavefront.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', Huygens principle (wavefronts)
solution.final_answer: Option A: spherical, converging to the focus of the mirror

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The power of a lens is measured in dioptres, a lens of focal length 1 m having a power of 1 D.
Statement II: A converging (convex) lens has a negative power.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Power of a lens P = 1/f (f in metres)
solution.explanation: P = 1/f, so 1 D = 1 m⁻¹ and a lens of focal length 1 m has a power of 1 D (Statement I true). A converging lens has a positive focal length and hence a positive power; a diverging lens has a negative power (Statement II false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II reverses the sign convention: it is the diverging lens whose power is negative.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', power of a lens
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each lens or instrument in List-I with the position of the object it uses, as described in List-II.

List-I:
A. Simple microscope forming its final image at the near point (object position relative to the lens)
B. Objective of a compound microscope (object position)
C. Objective of an astronomical telescope (object position)
D. Eyepiece of an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment (position of the intermediate image)

List-II:
I. Just beyond the focus of the lens
II. Between the focus and the lens
III. Practically at infinity
IV. Exactly at the focus of the lens

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Image formation in the simple microscope, compound microscope and telescope
solution.explanation: A simple microscope needs a virtual, magnified image, so the object is inside the focal length. The objective of a compound microscope forms a real, magnified image, so the object is placed just beyond its focus. A telescope views distant objects. In normal adjustment the final image is at infinity, so the intermediate image lies at the focus of the eyepiece.
steps: B: object just beyond f_o → I
D: intermediate image at f_e → IV
solution.why_others_wrong: A-I, B-II, ... interchanges the simple microscope and the objective of the compound microscope. A-II, B-IV, ... puts the microscope object exactly at the focus, where the image would be at infinity. A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III interchanges the telescope's object and intermediate image.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin convex lens forms an image twice the size of an object (magnification of magnitude 2) for two different positions of the object on its axis, one giving a real image and the other a virtual image. These two object positions are 10 cm apart. The focal length of the lens is:

solution.concept: Thin lens magnification m = v/u = f/(u + f) (Cartesian signs)
solution.explanation: For a real image m = −2 and for a virtual image m = +2. Using m = f/(u + f) gives the two object distances in terms of f, and their difference is f.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 cm and 5 cm take the separation of the two positions as half or twice the focal length. 15 cm is the object distance for the real image, not the focal length.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', thin lens formula; magnification

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin convex lens of focal length 15 cm forms a real image of a real object. The least possible distance between the object and its real image is:

solution.concept: For a real image by a convex lens, object–image distance D = u + v is least (= 4f) when u = v = 2f
solution.explanation: With the object at 2f the real image is at 2f on the other side, and moving the object either nearer to F or farther away only increases the total distance. So the least separation is 4f.
steps: D is least at u = v = 2f
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 cm is 2f, the distance of the object (or image) from the lens in that position. 15 cm is f itself. 45 cm has no basis: the separation never falls below 4f.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', thin lens formula

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: When unpolarised light in air falls on the plane surface of a transparent medium at an angle of incidence of 60°, the reflected light is completely plane polarised. The critical angle for light going from this medium into air is about:

solution.concept: Brewster's law tan i_B = n; critical angle sin C = 1/n
solution.explanation: The angle of incidence for completely polarised reflection is the Brewster angle, so the refractive index is tan 60° = √3. The critical angle then follows from sin C = 1/n.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30° takes the critical angle as 90° minus the Brewster angle. 60° takes it equal to the Brewster angle. 55° uses cos C = 1/n instead of sin C = 1/n.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation (Brewster's law)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Young's double-slit experiment the separation between the centres of the two slits is 1.0 mm. Each slit has a finite width a, and the single-slit diffraction pattern of each slit, observed on the same screen with the same light, has a central maximum (between its first minima on either side) that contains exactly 10 interference fringe widths. The width a of each slit is:

solution.concept: Linear width of the single-slit central maximum = 2λD/a; fringe width of the double slit = λD/d
solution.explanation: Setting the width of the central maximum equal to 10 fringe widths, λ and D cancel.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.1 mm takes the width of the central maximum as λD/a (half its true value). 0.4 mm fits only 5 fringe widths into the central maximum. 5 mm inverts the ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', diffraction (the single slit); interference of light waves and Young's experiment

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin convex lens of focal length 20 cm is placed in contact with a thin concave lens of focal length 30 cm. A small object is placed on the common axis, 30 cm in front of the combination. The image formed is:

options.text: 60 cm from the lenses, on the other side (real)
20 cm from the lenses, on the other side (real)
60 cm from the lenses, on the same side as the object (virtual)
30 cm from the lenses, on the same side as the object (virtual)

solution.concept: Thin lenses in contact: 1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂; thin lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/F
solution.explanation: The combination has 1/F = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60, a converging lens of focal length 60 cm. The object at 30 cm is inside this focal length, so the image is virtual.
steps: v = −60 cm: virtual, on the object's side
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 cm on the other side is a sign error in the lens formula. 20 cm on the other side treats the concave lens as converging (F = 12 cm). 30 cm on the object's side has no basis in the lens formula.
