solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', combination of thin lenses in contact
solution.final_answer: Option C: 60 cm from the lenses, on the same side as the object (virtual)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A real object is moved along the principal axis of a convex mirror from a very large distance up to the pole of the mirror. During this motion, the image:

options.text: moves from the pole towards the focus and shrinks in size
moves from the focus out to infinity, becoming larger than the object
stays at the focus, only its size increasing
moves from the focus towards the pole and grows in size, though it always stays smaller than the object

solution.concept: Image formation by a convex mirror (mirror equation with f > 0)
solution.explanation: For a distant object the image is a point-sized image at the focus behind the mirror. As the object approaches, 1/v = 1/f − 1/u gives a virtual image between the focus and the pole that moves towards the pole, and the magnification v/u grows towards +1 but never reaches it for a real object at a finite distance.
steps: As u → 0: v → 0 (towards the pole), m → 1
solution.why_others_wrong: The image moves towards the pole, not away from it, and grows rather than shrinks. A convex mirror never forms a magnified image of a real object or an image at infinity. The image does not stay at the focus.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors
solution.final_answer: Option D: moves from the focus towards the pole and grows in size, though it always stays smaller than the object

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When Young's double-slit experiment is performed with white light, the central fringe is white, while the fringes on either side of it are coloured.
Reason (R): Light waves are transverse waves.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Fringe width depends on wavelength (β = λD/d)
solution.explanation: At the centre the path difference is zero for every wavelength, so all colours give a maximum there and the central fringe is white. Elsewhere the positions of maxima depend on λ, so different colours separate and the fringes are coloured (A true). Light is indeed a transverse wave (R true), but this is shown by polarisation and has nothing to do with the colours of the fringes.
steps: Zero path difference for all λ → white centre
β ∝ λ → colours separate → coloured fringes
Transverse nature is unrelated → R not the explanation
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, but the colouring comes from the dependence of the fringe positions on wavelength, not from the transverse nature of light.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', interference of light waves and Young's experiment
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about interference and Young's double-slit experiment are correct?

(a) Two sources are coherent if the phase difference between the waves they send out stays constant in time.
(b) In Young's experiment, the two slits illuminated by light from a single source slit act as coherent sources.
(c) The fringe width does not depend on the intensity of the light used.
(d) When the two slits are equidistant from the source slit, the central fringe is dark.
(e) Dark fringes are formed at points where the waves from the two slits arrive in phase.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Coherence and the conditions for constructive and destructive interference
solution.explanation: Coherent sources keep a constant phase difference (a true). Young obtained such sources by letting the light from one slit fall on two slits, so that any phase change in the source affects both equally (b true). β = λD/d does not involve the intensity (c true). With the slits equidistant from the source slit, the waves reach the centre of the screen with zero path difference, giving a bright central fringe (d false). Dark fringes are where the waves arrive in opposite phase (e false).
steps: (d) false: zero path difference at the centre → bright
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (d) or (e) include a false statement; (a) and (b) only leaves out the true statement (c).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', coherent and incoherent addition of waves; interference of light waves and Young's experiment

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The power of a combination of thin lenses placed in contact is the algebraic sum of the powers of the individual lenses.
Statement II: When several lenses are used in combination, the total magnification produced is the product of the magnifications produced by the individual lenses.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Combination of thin lenses in contact
solution.explanation: For thin lenses in contact, 1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ + ..., so P = P₁ + P₂ + ... (Statement I true). The image formed by the first lens acts as the object for the second, so the sizes multiply: m = m₁m₂m₃... (Statement II true).
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are correct, so options calling either of them false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', combination of thin lenses in contact
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Light enters a transparent cube, placed in air, through one of its faces. The least refractive index of the material of the cube for which no ray that enters through that face, whatever its angle of incidence, can come out through an adjacent face (a face perpendicular to the first) is:

solution.concept: Refraction at the first face followed by total internal reflection at a perpendicular face
solution.explanation: A ray refracted at angle r into the cube meets the adjacent face at an angle of incidence 90° − r. The worst case is grazing incidence on the first face, when r is largest (sin r = 1/n). Total internal reflection at the adjacent face for this ray needs sin(90° − r) = cos r ≥ 1/n.
solution.why_others_wrong: √3, 1.5 and 2 all satisfy the condition, but the question asks for the least value, which is √2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A fish is 12 cm below the surface of still water (refractive index 4/3), and a bird is 18 cm above the surface, vertically above the fish. Using the near-normal (paraxial) approximation for refraction at a plane surface, the distance of the bird from the fish, as it appears to the fish looking straight up, is:

solution.concept: Refraction at a plane surface: for near-normal viewing, apparent distance = (n of observer's medium/n of object's medium) × real distance from the surface
solution.explanation: The fish sees the bird through the water surface. Light from the bird travels from air into water, so for an observer in water the bird appears farther from the surface by the factor 4/3. The fish's own distance from the surface is real and unchanged.
steps: Apparent height of the bird above the surface = (4/3) × 18 = 24 cm
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 cm is the real distance. 25.5 cm divides the bird's height by n, which is what the bird would see for the fish's depth, not what the fish sees. 40 cm also scales the fish's own distance from the surface.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction (real and apparent depth)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In an interference experiment, two coherent waves reach a point on the screen with intensities I and 4I. At a point where the phase difference between them is π/3, the intensity, expressed as a fraction of the maximum intensity I_max in the pattern, is:

solution.concept: Resultant intensity of two coherent waves: I = I₁ + I₂ + 2√(I₁I₂) cos φ
solution.explanation: The maximum occurs where cos φ = 1: I_max = (√I + √(4I))² = 9I. At φ = π/3, the interference term is 2 × 2I × ½ = 2I.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3I_max/4 uses cos²(φ/2), which holds only for two waves of equal intensity. 5I_max/9 drops the interference term, as if the waves were incoherent. I_max/9 is the minimum intensity (φ = π).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', coherent and incoherent addition of waves

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Young's double-slit experiment the slits are 1.0 mm apart. When the screen is moved 50 cm closer to the slits, the fringe width decreases by 0.30 mm. The wavelength of the light used is:

solution.concept: Fringe width β = λD/d is proportional to D, so Δβ = λΔD/d
solution.explanation: Only D changes. The change in fringe width is therefore λ/d times the change in D, so the original value of D is not needed.
solution.why_others_wrong: 300 nm divides by 1.0 m instead of 0.50 m. 1200 nm multiplies by the factor 2 instead of dividing. 60 nm is a power-of-ten slip in converting millimetres.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', interference of light waves and Young's experiment

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A ray of light entering one face of a glass slab with parallel faces, placed in air, can be totally internally reflected at the opposite face if its angle of incidence at the first face is made large enough.
Reason (R): Total internal reflection can occur only when light travels from an optically denser medium towards an optically rarer medium.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Refraction through a parallel slab; condition for total internal reflection
solution.explanation: At the first face sin i = n sin r. The faces are parallel, so the ray meets the second face at the same angle r, with n sin r = sin i ≤ 1. Hence the angle at the second face never exceeds the critical angle (sin r ≤ 1/n), and the ray always emerges, parallel to its original direction (A false). R correctly states one of the conditions for total internal reflection.
steps: Angle at the second face = r
n sin r = sin i ≤ 1 → r ≤ C
No total internal reflection → A false; R true
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so the options calling it true are wrong. Glass to air is denser to rarer, as R requires, but the geometry of a parallel slab never lets the angle at the second face exceed the critical angle.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A small real object is placed 30 cm from each of the optical elements in List-I, on its principal axis. Each element has a focal length of magnitude 20 cm. Match each element with the image it forms (List-II).

List-I:
A. Concave mirror
B. Convex mirror
C. Convex lens
D. Concave lens

List-II:
I. Real, 60 cm from the element, on the same side as the object
II. Virtual, 12 cm from the element, on the side opposite to the object
III. Real, 60 cm from the element, on the side opposite to the object
IV. Virtual, 12 cm from the element, on the same side as the object

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f and lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f with Cartesian signs
solution.explanation: A mirror sends light back, so a real image forms on the object's side and a virtual image behind it. A lens lets light through, so a real image forms on the far side and a virtual image on the object's side.
steps: Concave mirror (f = −20, u = −30): v = −60 cm → real, object side
Convex mirror (f = +20): v = +12 cm → virtual, behind the mirror
Convex lens (f = +20): v = +60 cm → real, far side
Concave lens (f = −20): v = −12 cm → virtual, object side
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes give the right distances but put the real or virtual images on the wrong side, mixing up how mirrors and lenses send light.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection by spherical mirrors; refraction by a lens
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following conclusions are obtained correctly from Huygens' principle applied to plane waves?

(a) For refraction, sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂, where v₁ and v₂ are the speeds of light in the two media.
(b) For reflection at a plane surface, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
(c) On refraction the frequency is unchanged, and the wavelength in each medium is proportional to the speed of light in it.
(d) When light passes from a rarer to a denser medium, the refracted wavefront travels faster than the incident wavefront.
(e) Secondary wavelets in any medium spread out with the speed of light in vacuum.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Huygens' construction for reflection and refraction of a plane wavefront
solution.explanation: During the time τ that the incident wavefront takes to sweep across the surface, the secondary wavelets in medium 2 grow to radius v₂τ, which gives sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂ (a true) and, for reflection, equal angles (b true). The frequency is fixed by the source, so λ = v/ν ∝ v (c true). Bending towards the normal (rarer to denser) means v₂ < v₁: the wave is slower in the denser medium (d false). The wavelets in a medium spread with the speed of light in that medium (e false).
steps: (d) false: slower in the denser medium
(e) false: wavelets move at v of the medium
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (d) or (e) include a false statement; (a) and (b) only leaves out the true statement (c).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', refraction and reflection of plane waves using Huygens principle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: The threshold wavelength for photoelectric emission from metal A is 600 nm. Metal B has a work function twice that of metal A. The threshold wavelength for metal B is:

solution.concept: Work function φ₀ = hν₀ = hc/λ₀
solution.explanation: The threshold wavelength is inversely proportional to the work function, so doubling the work function halves the threshold wavelength.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1200 nm makes λ₀ proportional to φ₀. 600 nm assumes the threshold wavelength is the same for all metals. 424 nm divides by √2 instead of 2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', photoelectric effect; Einstein's photoelectric equation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: The de Broglie wavelength of helium atoms in a gas, calculated with their rms speed (so that λ = h/√(3mkT)), is λ at 27 °C. At 927 °C it becomes:

solution.concept: de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p with p = √(3mkT) for thermal motion, so λ ∝ 1/√T (T in kelvin)
solution.explanation: The temperatures must be converted to kelvin: 27 °C = 300 K and 927 °C = 1200 K. The absolute temperature becomes four times, so the wavelength is halved.
solution.why_others_wrong: λ/5.9 uses the Celsius temperatures. λ/4 takes λ as inversely proportional to T instead of √T. 2λ makes the wavelength grow with temperature, though the atoms move faster.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: For a certain metal, the graph of the stopping potential V₀ (y-axis) against the frequency ν of the incident light (x-axis) is a straight line that cuts the frequency axis at 4.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz and has a slope of 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s. The stopping potential for light of frequency 9.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz, and the work function of the metal, are respectively:

solution.concept: Einstein's equation in the form V₀ = (h/e)ν − φ₀/e: slope h/e, frequency intercept ν₀ = φ₀/h
solution.explanation: The line passes through (ν₀, 0) with slope h/e, so V₀ = (h/e)(ν − ν₀). The work function in electron volts is (h/e)ν₀, i.e. the slope times the threshold frequency.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.6 V multiplies the slope by ν instead of (ν − ν₀), as if the line passed through the origin. 3.6 eV is the photon energy at 9.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz, not the work function. 1.6 V and 2.0 eV interchange the two results.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation: energy quantum of radiation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: Light containing only two wavelengths, 400 nm and 300 nm, falls on a metal surface whose work function is 2.1 eV. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, the stopping potential for the photoelectrons is about:

solution.concept: Einstein's photoelectric equation K_max = hν − φ₀; the stopping potential stops the fastest electrons
solution.explanation: To stop the photocurrent completely, the collector must turn back even the fastest photoelectrons, which are those ejected by the shorter wavelength (higher photon energy).
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 V is enough to stop only the electrons ejected by the 400 nm light. 1.5 V averages the two stopping potentials. 3.0 V adds the 1.0 V and 2.0 V values, but each electron absorbs a single photon.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation: energy quantum of radiation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When monochromatic light ejects photoelectrons from a metal, the emitted electrons have kinetic energies ranging from zero up to a maximum value.
Statement II: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons equals the whole energy hν of the incident photon.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Einstein's photoelectric equation K_max = hν − φ₀
solution.explanation: Each photon gives its energy hν to one electron. An electron must spend at least the work function φ₀ (more if it comes from deeper inside or loses energy on the way) to escape, so the emitted electrons have kinetic energies from zero up to K_max (Statement I true). Even the fastest electrons have spent φ₀, so K_max = hν − φ₀, less than hν (Statement II false).
steps: Energy needed to escape ≥ φ₀ → K from 0 to K_max → I true
K_max = hν − φ₀ < hν → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II leaves out the work function, which every photoelectron must spend to leave the metal.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation: energy quantum of radiation
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: Photons of the same energy fall on two metals: metal A of work function 2.0 eV and metal B of work function 3.5 eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons from A is twice that of the photoelectrons from B. The energy of each photon is:

solution.concept: Einstein's photoelectric equation K_max = E − φ₀ for each metal
solution.explanation: Write K_max for each metal with the same photon energy E and use the given ratio.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 eV is the difference of the work functions (it is K_B, not E). 5.5 eV adds the two work functions. 7.0 eV is twice the work function of B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation: energy quantum of radiation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
An electron and an alpha particle, both moving much slower than light, have the same de Broglie wavelength. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) They have momenta of equal magnitude.
(b) The electron has the larger kinetic energy.
(c) The electron has the larger speed.
(d) They have equal kinetic energies.
(e) If each was accelerated from rest through a potential difference, the electron was accelerated through the smaller potential difference.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: λ = h/p; K = p²/2m; for acceleration from rest qV = K
solution.explanation: Equal wavelengths mean equal momenta (a true). With the same p, the lighter electron has the larger speed p/m (c true) and the larger kinetic energy p²/2m (b true, d false). The electron's kinetic energy is thousands of times that of the alpha particle while its charge is only half as large, so it needed a much larger accelerating potential difference, V = K/q (e false).
steps: v = p/m, K = p²/2m: larger for the electron
V = K/q: V_e = p²/2m_e e ≫ V_α = p²/(2m_α × 2e)
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (d) or (e) include a false statement; (a) and (c) only leaves out the true statement (b).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A nuclear power station produces energy at the rate of 900 MW. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the mass converted into energy every second is:

solution.concept: Mass–energy equivalence E = mc²
solution.explanation: In one second 9 × 10⁸ J of energy is produced; the corresponding mass is E/c².
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.0 kg divides by c instead of c². 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ kg and 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ kg come from taking 1 MW as 10³ W or 10⁹ W.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', mass-energy and nuclear binding energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The wavelengths of the hydrogen spectrum are given by 1/λ = R(1/n_f² − 1/n_i²). Taking R = 1.1 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, the wavelength of the first line of the Paschen series (n_i = 4 → n_f = 3) and the region of the spectrum in which it lies are:

options.text: about 656 nm, in the visible region

solution.concept: Rydberg formula for the hydrogen spectrum; Paschen series ends on n = 3
solution.explanation: Substitute n_f = 3 and n_i = 4 for the first (longest-wavelength) line of the Paschen series.
solution.why_others_wrong: 656 nm is the first Balmer line (3 → 2). 0.82 µm is the series limit of the Paschen series (∞ → 3), not its first line. 1.87 µm is longer than visible wavelengths, so it lies in the infrared, not the ultraviolet.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', line spectra of the hydrogen atom
solution.final_answer: Option D: about 1.87 µm, in the infrared

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the energy level diagram of the hydrogen atom (E_n = −13.6/n² eV), as the principal quantum number n increases, the energy difference between successive levels:

options.text: decreases, the levels crowding closer together as E approaches zero
stays the same, 10.2 eV for every pair of successive levels

solution.concept: Energy levels of hydrogen: E_n ∝ −1/n²
solution.explanation: The gaps between successive levels are 10.2 eV (1 → 2), 1.89 eV (2 → 3), 0.66 eV (3 → 4) and so on, getting smaller and smaller. The levels crowd together just below E = 0, the ionisation limit.
steps: E₂ − E₁ = 10.2 eV, E₃ − E₂ = 1.89 eV, E₄ − E₃ = 0.66 eV
Gaps shrink → levels crowd towards E = 0
solution.why_others_wrong: The gaps shrink rather than grow or stay constant; 10.2 eV is only the gap between n = 1 and n = 2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom (energy levels)
solution.final_answer: Option B: decreases, the levels crowding closer together as E approaches zero

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Using 1/λ = R(1/n_f² − 1/n_i²) for hydrogen, the ratio of the shortest wavelength of the Lyman series to the shortest wavelength of the Paschen series is:

solution.concept: Shortest wavelength of a series: transition from n_i = ∞, so 1/λ = R/n_f²
solution.explanation: The series limit of each series corresponds to n_i → ∞, so λ_short = n_f²/R: 1/R for Lyman (n_f = 1) and 9/R for Paschen (n_f = 3).
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 : 1 inverts the ratio. 1 : 3 takes λ as proportional to n_f instead of n_f². 1 : 4 uses the Balmer series (n_f = 2) instead of Paschen.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', line spectra of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In one mode of fission, ²³⁵U absorbs a slow neutron and splits as ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴⁰₅₄Xe + ⁹⁴₃₈Sr + 2 ¹₀n. Take the binding energy per nucleon as 7.6 MeV for ²³⁵U and 8.4 MeV for each of the two fission fragments (a free neutron has no binding energy). The energy released in this fission is about:

solution.concept: Energy released = (total binding energy of products) − (total binding energy of reactants)
solution.explanation: Only the nucleons bound in nuclei contribute binding energy. The fragments contain 140 + 94 = 234 nucleons; the two neutrons released are free, as is the neutron absorbed.
solution.why_others_wrong: 196 MeV counts all 236 nucleons, including the free neutrons, as bound at 8.4 MeV. 188 MeV multiplies the difference in binding energy per nucleon (0.8 MeV) by 235, ignoring that the numbers of bound nucleons differ. 1966 MeV is the total binding energy of the fragments, not the energy released.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', nuclear energy (fission)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the ground state of the hydrogen atom in the Bohr model, the electron moves in a circle of radius 0.53 × 10⁻¹⁰ m with a speed of 2.2 × 10⁶ m/s. The time it takes to complete one revolution is about:

solution.concept: Uniform circular motion: T = 2πr/v
solution.explanation: The period is the circumference of the orbit divided by the speed of the electron.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁷ s is r/v, without the factor 2π. 7.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ s is the time for half a revolution (πr/v). 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ s uses 2π times the diameter.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a fusion reaction that releases energy, the total mass of the products is greater than the total mass of the reacting nuclei.
Reason (R): Fusion of very light nuclei releases energy because the binding energy per nucleon of the product nucleus is greater than that of the reacting nuclei.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Energy released in a nuclear reaction = (mass of reactants − mass of products) c²
solution.explanation: When two light nuclei fuse into a more tightly bound nucleus, the binding energy increases; the extra binding energy is released, and by E = mc² the products have less mass than the reactants (A false). R correctly gives the reason why fusion of light nuclei releases energy.
steps: Larger binding energy per nucleon of the product → R true
solution.why_others_wrong: A reverses the mass change: a reaction that releases energy always has products of smaller total mass.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', nuclear energy (fusion); mass-energy and nuclear binding energy
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The total energy of the electron in any Bohr orbit of the hydrogen atom is negative, which means that the electron is bound to the nucleus.
Statement II: As the principal quantum number n of the orbit increases, the total energy of the electron becomes more negative.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Energy of the electron in the Bohr model: E_n = −13.6/n² eV
solution.explanation: A negative total energy means that energy must be supplied to free the electron: it is bound (Statement I true). As n increases, E_n = −13.6/n² eV rises towards zero (−13.6, −3.4, −1.51 eV, ...), i.e. becomes less negative (Statement II false).
steps: E_n = −13.6/n²: larger n → closer to 0 → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II reverses the trend: the outer orbits have higher (less negative) energies, which is why energy must be absorbed to raise the electron to them.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The fusion reaction ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n releases 17.6 MeV, and the fission of a ²³⁵U nucleus after it absorbs a neutron releases about 200 MeV. Comparing the energy released per nucleon of the reacting particles (including the neutron absorbed in fission), the ratio of the value for this fusion reaction to that for fission is about:

solution.concept: Energy per nucleon of reactants = energy released/number of nucleons taking part
solution.explanation: The fusion reaction involves only 2 + 3 = 5 nucleons, while the fission involves 235 + 1 = 236 nucleons. Per nucleon, fusion releases several times more energy, although each fission event releases far more energy in total.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.09 and 11 compare the energies per reaction (17.6/200 and 200/17.6), not per nucleon. 1 assumes both processes release the same energy per nucleon.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', nuclear energy (fission and fusion)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, the radius of the nth orbit is proportional to n² and the speed of the electron in it is proportional to 1/n. The revolving electron is equivalent to a circular current loop. The ratio of the magnetic field produced at the nucleus by the electron in the n = 1 orbit to that produced by the electron in the n = 2 orbit is:

solution.concept: Equivalent current I = e/T = ev/(2πr); field at the centre of a loop B = µ₀I/(2r)
solution.explanation: Combine the two relations: B = µ₀ev/(4πr²). With v ∝ 1/n and r ∝ n², B ∝ (1/n)/n⁴ = 1/n⁵.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 : 1 is the ratio of the equivalent currents only, forgetting that the radius also changes in B = µ₀I/2r. 16 : 1 takes B ∝ 1/n⁴. 1 : 32 inverts the ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
The radius of a nucleus of mass number A is R = R₀A^(1/3). Match each property of the nucleus in List-I with the way it depends on A in List-II.

List-I:
A. Radius of the nucleus
B. Volume of the nucleus
C. Density of nuclear matter
D. Surface area of the nucleus

List-II:
I. Proportional to A
II. Proportional to A^(1/3)
III. Proportional to A^(2/3)
IV. Independent of A

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: R = R₀A^(1/3); volume ∝ R³; density = mass/volume with mass ∝ A
solution.explanation: The volume (4/3)πR³ is proportional to A. The mass is also proportional to A, so the density is the same for all nuclei. The surface area 4πR² is proportional to A^(2/3).
solution.why_others_wrong: A-II, B-III, ... interchanges the volume and the surface area. A-I, B-II, ... interchanges the radius and the volume. A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV interchanges the density and the surface area.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', size of the nucleus
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A singly ionised helium ion (He⁺, Z = 2) has its electron in the n = 2 orbit. In the Bohr model (E_n = −13.6 Z²/n² eV, r_n = 0.53 n²/Z Å, v_n ∝ Z/n), which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The total energy of the electron is −13.6 eV.
(b) The radius of the orbit is about 1.06 Å.
(c) The speed of the electron equals the speed of the electron in the ground state of the hydrogen atom.
(d) The orbital angular momentum of the electron is h/2π.
(e) In a transition to the n = 1 orbit, the ion emits a photon of energy 10.2 eV.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Bohr model for hydrogen-like ions
solution.explanation: E₂ = −13.6 × 4/4 = −13.6 eV (a true). r₂ = 0.53 × 4/2 = 1.06 Å (b true). v ∝ Z/n = 2/2 = 1, the same as for hydrogen with n = 1 (c true). The angular momentum is nh/2π = 2h/2π = h/π (d false). E₂ − E₁ = −13.6 − (−54.4) = 40.8 eV, four times the hydrogen value of 10.2 eV (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (d) or (e) include a false statement; (a) and (b) only leaves out the true statement (c).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A silicon diode is connected in series with a 1.5 kΩ resistor across a 3.7 V DC supply so that it is forward biased. Treating the diode as having a constant forward voltage drop of 0.7 V when it conducts, the power dissipated in the diode is:

solution.concept: Diode with a constant forward drop: I = (V − 0.7)/R; power in the diode = 0.7 V × I
solution.explanation: The resistor takes the supply voltage minus the diode's drop, which fixes the current. The diode dissipates its voltage drop times this current.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.0 mW is the power in the resistor and 7.4 mW the total power from the supply. 1.7 mW uses a current that ignores the diode's 0.7 V drop (3.7/1.5 kΩ).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', p-n junction diode under forward bias

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Silicon is doped with a trivalent impurity such as boron. In the energy band diagram of this p-type semiconductor, the acceptor energy level lies:

options.text: slightly below the bottom of the conduction band
slightly above the top of the valence band
exactly in the middle of the band gap

solution.concept: Energy bands of extrinsic semiconductors
solution.explanation: An acceptor atom readily accepts an electron from a neighbouring bond, leaving a hole. Very little energy is needed for this, so the acceptor level lies just above the top of the valence band.
steps: Acceptor: accepts an electron from the valence band easily
solution.why_others_wrong: Slightly below the conduction band is the donor level of an n-type semiconductor. The acceptor level is not at mid-gap and does not lie inside either band.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', extrinsic semiconductor (p-type)
solution.final_answer: Option B: slightly above the top of the valence band

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A p-n junction is forward biased when its p-side is connected to the positive terminal of a battery and its n-side to the negative terminal.
Statement II: When a p-n junction is reverse biased, its depletion region becomes wider.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Forward and reverse bias of a p-n junction
solution.explanation: Forward bias means the external voltage opposes the built-in barrier: p-side to the positive terminal (Statement I true). In reverse bias the applied voltage adds to the barrier and pulls the majority carriers away from the junction, so the depletion region widens (Statement II true).
steps: p → +, n → − : forward bias → I true
Reverse bias: barrier V₀ + V, depletion region wider → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are correct, so options calling either of them false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', p-n junction diode under forward bias; under reverse bias
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each item in List-I with the correct description in List-II.

List-I:
A. Energy band structure of a metal
B. Energy band gap of an insulator
C. Energy band gap of a semiconductor
D. Electrical behaviour of pure silicon at 0 K

List-II:
I. The conduction band is partly filled, or overlaps the valence band
II. Greater than 3 eV
III. Less than 3 eV
IV. It behaves as an insulator

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Classification of solids on the basis of energy bands
solution.explanation: In metals the conduction band is partly filled or overlaps the valence band, so electrons can move freely. Insulators have a large gap, Eg > 3 eV; semiconductors a small gap, Eg < 3 eV. At 0 K a pure semiconductor has its valence band full and conduction band empty, so it behaves as an insulator.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-I, B-III, ... interchanges the band gaps of insulators and semiconductors. A-IV, ... calls a metal an insulator. A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III mixes up the band gap of a semiconductor with the behaviour of pure silicon at 0 K.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', classification of metals, conductors and semiconductors (on the basis of energy bands)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The secondary of a transformer gives an alternating voltage of 12 V (rms). It feeds a half-wave rectifier made of a single silicon diode in series with a load resistor. Treating the diode as having a constant forward drop of 0.7 V when it conducts, the peak voltage across the load is about:

solution.concept: Peak value V₀ = √2 V_rms; the conducting diode takes away its forward drop
solution.explanation: The load receives the peak of the secondary voltage minus the diode's forward drop during the conducting half cycle.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.3 V subtracts the drop from the rms value instead of the peak. 17.0 V ignores the diode's drop. 15.6 V subtracts two diode drops, though only one diode conducts.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', application of junction diode as a rectifier

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A Zener diode of breakdown voltage 5.0 V is connected through a 100 Ω series resistor to a DC supply, and a 500 Ω load resistor is connected across the Zener diode. When the supply voltage is raised from 10 V to 12 V, the Zener diode remaining in breakdown, the current through the Zener diode:

solution.concept: Zener regulator: load voltage fixed at V_Z, so the load current is fixed; extra series current goes through the Zener
solution.explanation: The load voltage stays at 5.0 V, so the load current stays at 5.0/500 = 10 mA. The series resistor carries (V_in − 5.0)/100, which rises by 2 V/100 Ω = 20 mA, and all of this increase flows through the Zener diode.
steps: At 10 V: I_s = 50 mA, I_L = 10 mA, I_Z = 40 mA
At 12 V: I_s = 70 mA, I_L = 10 mA, I_Z = 60 mA
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 mA divides the 2 V change by the load resistance, but the load voltage does not change. The Zener current does change, because the series current changes. 3.3 mA divides the 2 V change by 600 Ω, treating the resistors as if they were in series without the Zener diode.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', Zener diode as a voltage regulator

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two ideal batteries, of 5 V and 3 V, have their negative terminals earthed. The positive terminal of each is connected to the anode of its own ideal diode, and the cathodes of the two diodes are joined at a point P. P is connected to earth through a 1 kΩ resistor. The current through the resistor and the current through the diode connected to the 3 V battery are, respectively:

solution.concept: Ideal diode: conducts with zero drop when forward biased, no current when reverse biased
solution.explanation: If the diode from the 5 V battery conducts, P is at 5 V. The diode from the 3 V battery then has its cathode at 5 V and its anode at 3 V, so it is reverse biased and carries no current. All the current comes from the 5 V battery.
steps: P at 5 V (via the conducting diode)
3 V diode: anode 3 V < cathode 5 V → off
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 mA and 3 mA assume both diodes conduct and their currents add. 4 mA and 2 mA put P at the average of the two emfs. 3 mA and 3 mA let the lower voltage set the potential of P.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', p-n junction diode under forward bias; under reverse bias

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A light emitting diode made of gallium arsenide (GaAs), whose band gap is about 1.4 eV, emits infrared rather than visible light.
Reason (R): The energy of the photons emitted by an LED is about equal to the band gap of its semiconductor, and photons of energy 1.4 eV have a wavelength of about 890 nm, longer than the wavelengths of visible light.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: LED: emitted photon energy ≈ band gap Eg; λ = hc/Eg
solution.explanation: In an LED, electrons recombining with holes across the band gap emit photons of energy close to Eg. For Eg ≈ 1.4 eV, λ ≈ 1240/1.4 ≈ 890 nm, beyond the red end of the visible spectrum (about 700 nm), so GaAs is used for infrared LEDs. R gives exactly this reason.
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the photon energy fixed by the band gap is the reason the light is infrared, so R is the correct explanation of A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', optoelectronic junction devices (light emitting diode)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: An AND gate followed by a NOT gate behaves as a NAND gate.
Statement II: A two-input OR gate with both its inputs joined together behaves as a NOT gate.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Truth tables of the basic gates
solution.explanation: Inverting the output of an AND gate gives NOT(A·B), which is the NAND function (Statement I true). With both inputs of an OR gate joined, the output is A + A = A: the input is passed on unchanged, not inverted (Statement II false). It is a NAND or NOR gate with joined inputs that acts as a NOT gate.
steps: A + A = A (not Ā) → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II confuses the OR gate with the NOR gate; joining the inputs of an OR gate gives no inversion.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A two-input logic gate (or combination of gates) gives an output of 1 when both inputs are 0, and an output of 0 when both inputs are 1. Which of the following could it be?

(a) A NAND gate
(b) A NOR gate
(c) An OR gate
(d) An AND gate
(e) An OR gate followed by a NOT gate

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Truth tables of OR, AND, NAND and NOR
solution.explanation: NAND gives 1 for (0, 0) and 0 for (1, 1) (a true). NOR also gives 1 for (0, 0) and 0 for (1, 1) (b true), and an OR gate followed by a NOT gate is a NOR gate (e true). OR gives 0 for (0, 0) (c false), and AND gives 1 for (1, 1) (d false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (c) or (d) include a gate that fails one of the two conditions; (a) and (b) only, or (a) and (e) only, leave out a gate that satisfies both.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal 12 V battery is connected across two branches in parallel. Branch 1 has a 2 kΩ resistor (joined to the positive terminal) and a 4 kΩ resistor in series, meeting at point B. Branch 2 has a 4 kΩ resistor (joined to the positive terminal) and a 2 kΩ resistor in series, meeting at point D. An ideal diode is connected with its anode at B and its cathode at D. The current through the diode is:

options.text: zero, because the diode is reverse biased

solution.concept: Ideal diode as a closed switch when forward biased; Kirchhoff's rules
solution.explanation: Without the diode, B would be at 12 × 4/6 = 8 V and D at 12 × 2/6 = 4 V, so the diode is forward biased and conducts, joining B and D. Then the two upper resistors (2 kΩ and 4 kΩ) are in parallel, and so are the two lower ones (4 kΩ and 2 kΩ), each pair being 4/3 kΩ, so the joined point is at 6 V. The diode current is the current arriving at B through the 2 kΩ resistor minus that leaving B through the 4 kΩ resistor.
steps: Open: V_B = 8 V > V_D = 4 V → diode conducts
I(2 kΩ, top of branch 1) = 6/2 = 3.0 mA; I(4 kΩ, bottom of branch 1) = 6/4 = 1.5 mA
Diode current = 3.0 − 1.5 = 1.5 mA, from B to D
solution.why_others_wrong: The diode is forward biased (B is at the higher potential), so zero is wrong. 2.0 mA divides the open-circuit 4 V difference by 2 kΩ. 3.0 mA is the current in the upper resistor of branch 1, part of which continues through the 4 kΩ resistor below B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', p-n junction diode under forward bias
solution.final_answer: Option C: 1.5 mA, from B to D

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An LED operates with a forward voltage of 2.0 V and a current of 20 mA, and emits light of wavelength 620 nm. 10% of the electrical power supplied to it is converted into this light. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm and 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, the number of photons it emits per second is about:

solution.concept: Photon emission rate = optical power/(energy per photon), with E = hc/λ
solution.explanation: The electrical power is VI. Only 10% of it emerges as light. Dividing the light power by the energy of one photon gives the number of photons per second.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.25 × 10¹⁷ assumes all the electrical power becomes light. 1.25 × 10¹⁵ takes the efficiency as 1%. 2.5 × 10¹⁶ uses half the correct photon energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', optoelectronic junction devices (light emitting diode)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Each circuit in List-I has inputs A and B. Match it with its outputs in List-II, listed for the inputs (A, B) = (0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1) in that order.

List-I:
A. A is passed through a NOT gate, and its output and B are fed to an AND gate
B. B is passed through a NOT gate, and A and its output are fed to an AND gate
C. A is passed through a NOT gate, and its output and B are fed to an OR gate
D. A and B are each passed through a NOT gate, and the two outputs are fed to an AND gate

List-II:
I. 0, 1, 0, 0
II. 0, 0, 1, 0
III. 1, 1, 0, 1
IV. 1, 0, 0, 0

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Truth tables of combinations of NOT, AND and OR gates
solution.explanation: Work out each Boolean expression for the four input pairs: Ā·B is 1 only for (0, 1); A·B̄ only for (1, 0); Ā + B is 0 only for (1, 0); Ā·B̄ is 1 only for (0, 0) (it is the NOR function).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange the first two circuits (inverting the wrong input) or the last two (confusing the OR and AND combinations).
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Inputs A and B are fed to a NAND gate, whose output is X. X is fed to both inputs of a second NAND gate, whose output is Y. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Y = A·B, i.e. the circuit as a whole behaves as an AND gate.
(b) X = 1 when A = 0 and B = 1.
(c) Y = 0 when A = 1 and B = 0.
(d) The circuit as a whole behaves as an OR gate.
(e) If the second gate is removed and X is taken as the output, the circuit behaves as an AND gate.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: NAND as a universal gate: a NAND with joined inputs is a NOT gate
solution.explanation: X = NOT(A·B). The second NAND has both inputs equal to X, so Y = NOT(X·X) = NOT X = A·B: an AND gate (a true, d false). For (0, 1), A·B = 0 so X = 1 (b true). For (1, 0), Y = A·B = 0 (c true). X alone is the NAND function, not AND (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (d) or (e) include a false statement; (a) and (b) only leaves out the true statement (c).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale, and has no zero error. While a wire is held between the studs, the 4 mm mark of the main (linear) scale is visible and so is the 0.5 mm mark just beyond it; the 18th division of the circular scale is on the reference line. The diameter of the wire is:

solution.concept: Screw gauge reading = main scale reading + (circular scale division × least count); least count = pitch/number of circular divisions
solution.explanation: The least count is 0.5 mm/50 = 0.01 mm. Since the half-millimetre mark beyond 4 mm is also uncovered, the main scale reading is 4.5 mm.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.18 mm misses the visible half-millimetre mark. 4.59 mm takes the least count as 0.005 mm. 4.36 mm misses the half-millimetre mark and takes the least count as 0.02 mm.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, Experimental Skills: screw gauge

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the resonance-tube experiment to find the speed of sound in air, an end correction has to be added to the length of the air column because:

options.text: the node at the water surface is formed slightly below the water surface
the speed of sound in the tube is greater than in the open air
the tuning fork is held slightly above the open end of the tube
the antinode at the open end of the tube is formed slightly outside (above) the open end

solution.concept: Resonance in a tube closed at one end; end correction e ≈ 0.3d
solution.explanation: The water surface is a rigid closed end, so the node forms right at it. At the open end, the air just outside also takes part in the vibration, so the displacement antinode lies a little beyond the end of the tube. The effective length of the vibrating column is therefore l + e.
steps: Closed end (water surface): node exactly at the surface
Open end: antinode slightly outside → l_eff = l + e
solution.why_others_wrong: The node is at the water surface itself, not below it. The speed of sound is the same inside and outside the tube. The position of the fork does not create the correction.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, Experimental Skills: speed of sound in air at room temperature using a resonance tube
solution.final_answer: Option D: the antinode at the open end of the tube is formed slightly outside (above) the open end

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the capillary-rise experiment, water rises to a vertical height of 3.0 cm in a long, clean capillary tube held vertical. If the same tube is instead held inclined at 60° to the vertical, the length of the water column in the tube becomes:

solution.concept: Capillary rise h = 2S cos θ/(rρg) fixes the vertical height of the column
solution.explanation: The vertical height to which the water rises depends only on the surface tension, contact angle, radius and density, not on the tilt of the tube. In the tilted tube the column must be longer to reach the same vertical height: l cos 60° = h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.0 cm assumes the length stays the same, which would give a smaller vertical height. 1.5 cm multiplies by cos 60° instead of dividing. 3.5 cm divides by sin 60°, measuring the angle from the wrong reference line.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, Experimental Skills: surface tension of water by capillary rise

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a resonance-tube experiment with a tuning fork of frequency 500 Hz, the first resonance is obtained when the air column is 15.8 cm long. The internal diameter of the tube is 4.0 cm, and the end correction may be taken as 0.3 times the diameter. The speed of sound in air is:

solution.concept: First resonance of a tube closed at one end: l₁ + e = λ/4
solution.explanation: Add the end correction to the measured length to get a quarter wavelength, then use v = fλ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 316 m/s leaves out the end correction. 364 m/s takes the end correction as 0.6 times the diameter instead of 0.6 times the radius. 170 m/s treats the first resonance length as λ/2.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, Experimental Skills: speed of sound in air at room temperature using a resonance tube

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the experiment to find the coefficient of viscosity of a liquid from the terminal velocity of a falling steel ball, the ball should be dropped along the axis of a wide jar, well away from its walls.
Reason (R): Stokes' law, F = 6πηrv, applies to a sphere moving through a liquid that extends far on all sides; near the walls of the jar the motion of the ball is affected and the law no longer holds.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Conditions for Stokes' law in the terminal-velocity experiment
solution.explanation: The terminal velocity is used with Stokes' law, which assumes the liquid extends far around the ball. Close to the walls, the liquid cannot flow freely round the ball, which slows it and gives a wrong value of η. That is why the ball is dropped along the axis of a wide jar: R explains A.
steps: Stokes' law assumes a liquid extending far around the sphere
Walls disturb the flow → wrong η
So the ball is dropped along the axis → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the validity of Stokes' law is the very reason for the precaution, so R is the correct explanation of A.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, Experimental Skills: coefficient of viscosity of a liquid by measuring the terminal velocity of a spherical body
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: To find the specific heat capacity of a liquid by the method of mixtures, a 200 g copper block at 100 °C (specific heat capacity of copper 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is dropped into 100 g of the liquid at 20 °C, contained in a calorimeter whose water equivalent is 10 g. The final steady temperature is 40 °C. Taking the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and neglecting heat losses to the surroundings, the specific heat capacity of the liquid is:

solution.concept: Principle of calorimetry: heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the liquid and the calorimeter
solution.explanation: The copper cools from 100 °C to 40 °C. The heat it gives out warms both the liquid and the calorimeter (treated as 10 g of water) from 20 °C to 40 °C.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ ignores the heat taken by the calorimeter. 2780 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ takes the copper's fall in temperature as 80 °C (100 − 20) instead of 60 °C. 2180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ adds the 10 g water equivalent to the mass of the liquid, as if the calorimeter had the liquid's specific heat.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, Experimental Skills: specific heat capacity of a given liquid by the method of mixtures

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each graph obtained in a laboratory experiment (List-I) with the description of its shape (List-II).

List-I:
A. Reverse-bias characteristic of a Zener diode (reverse current against reverse voltage)
B. Forward-bias characteristic of a p-n junction diode (current against voltage)
C. Angle of deviation against angle of incidence for a triangular glass prism
D. Image distance against object distance (magnitudes) for a convex lens forming real images

List-II:
I. A curve that falls to a minimum and then rises again
II. Current nearly zero until a particular reverse voltage, beyond which it rises very sharply at almost constant voltage
III. Current negligible up to a threshold voltage, then rising steeply and non-linearly
IV. A curve that approaches the lines u = f and v = f asymptotically (a rectangular hyperbola)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Shapes of characteristic and experimental graphs
solution.explanation: A Zener diode in reverse bias carries almost no current until its breakdown voltage, where the current rises sharply at nearly constant voltage. A junction diode in forward bias conducts appreciably only beyond the threshold (knee) voltage. The prism's deviation falls to a minimum and then rises. For a convex lens, (u − f)(v − f) = f², a rectangular hyperbola with asymptotes u = f and v = f.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-III, B-II, ... interchanges the Zener reverse and diode forward characteristics. The codes with C-IV, D-I interchange the prism and lens graphs.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, Experimental Skills: characteristic curves of a p-n junction diode and a Zener diode; i–δ curve of a prism; focal length of a convex lens
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV
